checks.explanation: Equity markets did rally in the weeks following this February 2023 episode, continuing gains into early 2023 before the March SVB-driven volatility.
In hindsight, 2023 achieved what was widely characterized as a soft landing, with growth continuing and inflation cooling without a formal recession.

The Fed funds rate actually peaked at 5.25-5.50%, higher than the predicted 4.75-5.0%, and the Fed did not deliver the predicted roughly 50 basis points of cuts over the following two years, instead holding rates elevated until September 2024.
Public SaaS valuation multiples did not return to the extreme 2021 bubble levels and instead settled into a lower, more historically normal range.

Rather than a record pace of deployment, venture capital deployment actually slowed significantly in the following years as firms became more cautious, leaving substantial dry powder undeployed longer than historically typical.
Venture capital deployment pace slowed dramatically in the years following this prediction, consistent with a multi-year, multi-fold slowdown in annual investment volume.
The fundraising environment for new, small, solo-capitalist, and micro-VC funds became significantly harder in the years following, with many such vehicles struggling or disappearing.
Apple's cumulative shareholder distributions via dividends and buybacks easily surpassed $1 trillion well before the end of 2025, given its long history of large-scale buybacks.
Meta significantly ramped up share buybacks and initiated dividends starting in 2024, putting it on a path to return several hundred billion dollars to shareholders across the 2023-2028 window.
While notable startup failures occurred in 2023-2024, the overall wave was not clearly documented as exceeding the severity of the 2008 financial crisis for startups broadly.
There is no comprehensive, verifiable data confirming that exactly around 50% of the referenced 2019-2022 seed and Series A/B cohort has gone out of business.
There is no comprehensive dataset confirming a specific 50-60% mortality rate for the referenced startup cohort.
The second half of 2023 and 2024 did see a well-documented major startup funding crunch as companies that delayed fundraising confronted much tougher market conditions.
As with the related prediction, this funding crunch materialized broadly as described, including widespread down rounds and difficult fundraises.
Startups with venture debt did face pressure from lenders during the tighter funding period, though this was not universally documented as lenders systematically collecting before cash ran out.
The startup ecosystem experienced widespread down rounds, restructurings, and recapitalizations through 2023 and 2024 as predicted.
SaaS valuation multiples generally recovered somewhat but remained well below the roughly 16x levels of the 2021 bubble peak.
SaaS multiples did not return to the elevated 12-16x levels of the 2021 bubble in the following years.
Interest rates did not return to near-zero, and 2021-bubble-magnitude valuation multiples did not reoccur in the following years.
Operating conditions remained difficult for many startups through roughly mid-2024 to early 2025, consistent with the predicted rough 18-24 month stretch.
No formal recession occurred in the U.S. during 2023; the economy achieved a soft landing instead.
Capital availability for startups remained structurally tighter than the 2021 environment for an extended period, without reverting to easy 2021-style funding conditions.
